Entropic Regularization: Sinkhorn Algorithm

Entropic regularization makes optimal transport smooth, strictly convex and scalable. This chapter first explains the discrete KL-regularized problem, derives Sinkhorn’s alternating matrix scaling algorithm, and then rewrites the same construction as a relative-entropy projection problem. It then records the general continuous formulation, develops the dual soft-transform picture, explains the path-space Schrodinger problem behind the static coupling formulation, and presents the main convex regularization variants and the debiased Sinkhorn divergence. A final section records a less standard viewpoint: after fixing the potential gauge, the finite-dimensional Sinkhorn equations admit a local holomorphic continuation to complex values of the temperature.

The presentation connects the older matrix-scaling literature Sinkhorn, 1964Sinkhorn & Knopp, 1967Sinkhorn, 1967 with modern entropic OT Cuturi, 2013Peyré & Cuturi, 2017.

Guiding Comparison

The unregularized Kantorovich problem is a linear program. Entropy replaces it by a smooth strictly convex problem whose optimizer has the scaling form P=diag⁡(u)Kdiag⁡(v)P=\operatorname{diag}(u)K\operatorname{diag}(v)P=diag(u)Kdiag(v). The cost is a biased OT approximation, but the payoff is differentiability and matrix-vector iterations.

Entropic Regularization for Discrete Measures¶

Entropy turns a possibly non-unique linear program into a unique smooth problem. The price is bias, but the reward is differentiability and fast scaling algorithms.

Definition: Discrete Shannon--Boltzmann Entropy

For a nonnegative matrix PPP, its Shannon--Boltzmann entropy is

H(P):=−∑i,jPi,jlog⁡Pi,j,H(P) \eqdef -\sum_{i,j}P_{i,j}\log P_{i,j},H(P):=−i,j∑​Pi,j​logPi,j​,
(1)

with the convention 0log⁡0=00\log 0=00log0=0.

Using this entropy as a regularizing function gives the approximate transport value

LCϵ(a,b):=min⁡P∈U(a,b)⟨P,C⟩−ϵH(P).\mathcal{L}_{C}^{\epsilon}(a,b) \eqdef \min_{P\in\mathbf{U}(a,b)} \langle P,C\rangle - \epsilon H(P).LCϵ​(a,b):=P∈U(a,b)min​⟨P,C⟩−ϵH(P).
(2)

Equivalently, the regularizer is ϵ∑i,jPi,jlog⁡Pi,j\epsilon\sum_{i,j}P_{i,j}\log P_{i,j}ϵ∑i,j​Pi,j​logPi,j​. It penalizes concentrated couplings and makes the objective strictly convex on the relative interior of the transport polytope.

Proposition: Existence and Uniqueness of Entropic OT

Assume that a,ba,ba,b are probability histograms and that CCC is finite. For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, problem (2) admits a unique minimizer. If all entries of aaa and bbb are positive, then this minimizer is positive on every entry.

Proof

The transport polytope is non-empty and compact, and the objective is continuous with the convention 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0, so a minimizer exists. On the relative interior,

−∂2H(P)=diag⁡(1/Pi,j)-\partial^2 H(P)=\operatorname{diag}(1/P_{i,j})−∂2H(P)=diag(1/Pi,j​)
(3)

is positive definite on every non-zero feasible direction. Hence −H-H−H is strictly convex on the polytope, which gives uniqueness.

If ai,bj>0a_i,b_j>0ai​,bj​>0 and a minimizer had Pi,j=0P_{i,j}=0Pi,j​=0, then the perturbation Pt=(1−t)P+t a⊗bP_t=(1-t)P+t\,a\otimes bPt​=(1−t)P+ta⊗b remains feasible for small t>0t>0t>0. The derivative of rlog⁡rr\log rrlogr at zero along a positive direction is −∞-\infty−∞, so the objective decreases, contradicting optimality.

Smoothing Effect¶

The entropy acts as a barrier for positivity and makes LCϵ(a,b)\mathcal{L}_{C}^{\epsilon}(a,b)LCϵ​(a,b) smooth in aaa, bbb, and CCC as long as these variables stay in the relative interior. As ϵ→+∞\epsilon\to+\inftyϵ→+∞, the minimizer converges to the independent coupling a⊗ba\otimes ba⊗b; as ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0, it approaches the optimal face of the original transport linear program.

show_book_figure("sinkhorn-entropy-lp-geometry")

Entropic regularization and slack barriers. Large ϵ\epsilonϵ selects an interior reference point, while small ϵ\epsilonϵ moves the minimizer toward a low-cost face of the transport polytope. The second row gives the analogous entropy-on-slacks picture for a generic linear program.

Entropy Barriers Versus Generic LP Barriers¶

For a generic linear program min⁡zℓ⊤z\min_z \ell^\top zminz​ℓ⊤z with constraints Az≤bAz\le bAz≤b, one can introduce positive slacks s=b−Azs=b-Azs=b−Az and penalize them by an entropy. This is a useful analogy, but it is not the standard self-concordant interior-point barrier. The canonical barrier is the Burg, or reverse-KL, barrier −∑ilog⁡si-\sum_i\log s_i−∑i​logsi​, which leads to Newton systems.

Optimal transport is special because entropy is placed on the entries of PPP, while the constraints are only row and column marginals. This separable structure turns Bregman projections into diagonal rescalings, giving the Sinkhorn iterations.

Sinkhorn’s Algorithm¶

Sinkhorn’s algorithm is alternating normalization of rows and columns. The key point is that the optimizer of the entropic problem has a multiplicative scaling form.

Proposition: Scaling Form of Entropic OT

PPP is the unique solution of (2) if and only if there exist nonnegative vectors u∈R+nu\in\RR_+^nu∈R+n​ and v∈R+mv\in\RR_+^mv∈R+m​ such that

Pi,j=uiKi,jvj,Ki,j:=exp⁡(−Ci,j/ϵ),P_{i,j}=u_iK_{i,j}v_j, \qquad K_{i,j}\eqdef\exp(-C_{i,j}/\epsilon),Pi,j​=ui​Ki,j​vj​,Ki,j​:=exp(−Ci,j​/ϵ),
(4)

and P∈U(a,b)P\in\mathbf{U}(a,b)P∈U(a,b).

Proof

After removing zero-mass rows and columns, the minimizer is strictly positive, so the positivity constraint can be ignored in the first-order conditions. Introduce Lagrange multipliers f∈Rnf\in\RR^nf∈Rn and g∈Rmg\in\RR^mg∈Rm for the two marginal constraints. The Lagrangian is

L(P,f,g)=⟨P,C⟩+ϵ∑i,jPi,jlog⁡Pi,j+⟨f,a−P1⟩+⟨g,b−P⊤1⟩.\mathcal{L}(P,f,g) = \langle P,C\rangle + \epsilon\sum_{i,j}P_{i,j}\log P_{i,j} + \langle f,a-P\mathbf 1\rangle + \langle g,b-P^\top\mathbf 1\rangle .L(P,f,g)=⟨P,C⟩+ϵi,j∑​Pi,j​logPi,j​+⟨f,a−P1⟩+⟨g,b−P⊤1⟩.
(5)

Stationarity with respect to Pi,jP_{i,j}Pi,j​ gives

Ci,j+ϵ(log⁡Pi,j+1)−fi−gj=0.C_{i,j} + \epsilon(\log P_{i,j}+1) - f_i-g_j =0.Ci,j​+ϵ(logPi,j​+1)−fi​−gj​=0.
(6)

Thus Pi,j=exp⁡((fi+gj−Ci,j)/ϵ−1)P_{i,j}=\exp((f_i+g_j-C_{i,j})/\epsilon-1)Pi,j​=exp((fi​+gj​−Ci,j​)/ϵ−1), which is exactly the scaling form after absorbing the one-body terms into uuu and vvv.

In matrix notation, P=diag⁡(u)Kdiag⁡(v)P=\operatorname{diag}(u)K\operatorname{diag}(v)P=diag(u)Kdiag(v). The marginal constraints become

u⊙(Kv)=a,v⊙(K⊤u)=b.u\odot(Kv)=a, \qquad v\odot(K^\top u)=b.u⊙(Kv)=a,v⊙(K⊤u)=b.
(7)

Solving each equation in turn gives Sinkhorn’s algorithm:

u(ℓ+1)=aKv(ℓ),v(ℓ+1)=bK⊤u(ℓ+1).u^{(\ell+1)} = \frac{a}{Kv^{(\ell)}}, \qquad v^{(\ell+1)} = \frac{b}{K^\top u^{(\ell+1)}}.u(ℓ+1)=Kv(ℓ)a​,v(ℓ+1)=K⊤u(ℓ+1)b​.
(8)

The division is entrywise. The scaling vectors are not unique: multiplying uuu by λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 and vvv by 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ leaves PPP unchanged.

Complexity bounds for Sinkhorn and comparisons with accelerated first-order methods are discussed in Altschuler et al., 2017Dvurechensky et al., 2018Knight, 2008. For a dense n×mn\times mn×m problem, each iteration costs one multiplication by KKK and one by K⊤K^\topK⊤, so the cost scales like CnmCnmCnm for CCC iterations. For fixed positive ϵ\epsilonϵ, the marginal error eventually has a linear regime, but small ϵ\epsilonϵ makes the Gibbs kernel more peaked and scaling harder.

Remark: Separable Gaussian kernels on grids

When the samples lie on a Cartesian grid and c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2, the Gibbs kernel is Gaussian and factorizes along coordinates. If the grid has qqq points per axis in dimension ddd, so that N=qdN=q^dN=qd grid points are used, then

K(x,y)=exp⁡ ⁣(−∥x−y∥2ϵ)=∏ℓ=1dexp⁡ ⁣(−(xℓ−yℓ)2ϵ).K(x,y)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\norm{x-y}^2}{\epsilon}\right) = \prod_{\ell=1}^d \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x_\ell-y_\ell)^2}{\epsilon}\right).K(x,y)=exp(−ϵ∥x−y∥2​)=ℓ=1∏d​exp(−ϵ(xℓ​−yℓ​)2​).
(9)

Multiplication by KKK can therefore be applied by successively multiplying along each coordinate direction, equivalently by applying one-dimensional Gaussian kernel operators along the axes. On a periodic or sufficiently padded uniform grid these are literal discrete convolutions. A direct dense one-dimensional multiplication costs O(q2)O(q^2)O(q2) on each of the qd−1q^{d-1}qd−1 coordinate lines, and this is repeated for ddd axes. Hence one Sinkhorn half-step costs

O(d qd+1)=O(d N1+1/d)O(d\,q^{d+1})=O(d\,N^{1+1/d})O(dqd+1)=O(dN1+1/d)
(10)

instead of O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2). With FFT-based or truncated Gaussian convolutions, the same separability can be pushed further, but the simple tensor-product estimate already explains why grid-based Sinkhorn can scale much better than a generic dense coupling.

Algorithm: Sinkhorn scaling

Input: Weights a,b\a,\ba,b, cost matrix C\CC, regularization ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, tolerance tol\mathrm{tol}tol.

Output: Entropic coupling P\PP.

Initialize: Set Kij=e−Cij/ϵ\K_{ij}=e^{-\C_{ij}/\epsilon}Kij​=e−Cij​/ϵ, v(0)=1m\vD^{(0)}=\ones_mv(0)=1m​, r0=+∞r_0=+\inftyr0​=+∞, and k=0k=0k=0.

While rk>tolr_k>\mathrm{tol}rk​>tol do:

Set k←k+1k\leftarrow k+1k←k+1.

u(k)=aKv(k−1).\uD^{(k)}=\frac{\a}{\K\vD^{(k-1)}}.u(k)=Kv(k−1)a​.

v(k)=bK⊤u(k).\vD^{(k)}=\frac{\b}{\transp{\K}\uD^{(k)}}.v(k)=K⊤u(k)b​.

P(k)=diag⁡(u(k))Kdiag⁡(v(k)).\P^{(k)}=\diag(\uD^{(k)})\K\diag(\vD^{(k)}).P(k)=diag(u(k))Kdiag(v(k)).

Set rk=max⁡{∥P(k)1m−a∥1,∥(P(k))⊤1n−b∥1}r_k=\max\{\norm{\P^{(k)}\ones_m-\a}_1,\norm{(\P^{(k)})^\top\ones_n-\b}_1\}rk​=max{∥∥​P(k)1m​−a∥∥​1​,∥∥​(P(k))⊤1n​−b∥∥​1​}.

Return P(k)\P^{(k)}P(k).

Reformulation Using Relative Entropy¶

The KL formulation identifies Sinkhorn as a projection method. It also prepares the continuous and unbalanced settings, where a reference measure is essential.

Definition: Discrete Relative Entropy

For nonnegative matrices P,QP,QP,Q of the same size, the generalized relative entropy is

KL⁡(P∣Q):=∑i,jPi,jlog⁡Pi,jQi,j−Pi,j+Qi,j.\operatorname{KL}(P|Q) \eqdef \sum_{i,j} P_{i,j}\log\frac{P_{i,j}}{Q_{i,j}} - P_{i,j} + Q_{i,j}.KL(P∣Q):=i,j∑​Pi,j​logQi,j​Pi,j​​−Pi,j​+Qi,j​.
(11)

The convention is 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0, and KL⁡(P∣Q)=+∞\operatorname{KL}(P|Q)=+\inftyKL(P∣Q)=+∞ if Qi,j=0Q_{i,j}=0Qi,j​=0 but Pi,j>0P_{i,j}>0Pi,j​>0 for some entry.

For matrices with the same total mass, the affine terms cancel and

KL⁡(P∣Q)=∑i,jPi,jlog⁡Pi,jQi,j.\operatorname{KL}(P|Q) = \sum_{i,j}P_{i,j}\log\frac{P_{i,j}}{Q_{i,j}}.KL(P∣Q)=i,j∑​Pi,j​logQi,j​Pi,j​​.
(12)

On fixed-mass couplings, taking Q=1n×mQ=\mathbf 1_{n\times m}Q=1n×m​ is equivalent to subtracting the Shannon--Boltzmann entropy. Taking the tensor-product reference gives the normalized formulation

min⁡P∈U(a,b)⟨P,C⟩+ϵKL⁡(P∣a⊗b).\min_{P\in\mathbf U(a,b)} \langle P,C\rangle + \epsilon\operatorname{KL}(P|a\otimes b).P∈U(a,b)min​⟨P,C⟩+ϵKL(P∣a⊗b).
(13)
Proposition: Relative Entropy is Distance-Like

Let P,Q∈R+n×mP,Q\in\RR_+^{n\times m}P,Q∈R+n×m​ have the same total mass and assume Qi,j>0Q_{i,j}>0Qi,j​>0 on the support of PPP. Then KL⁡(P∣Q)≥0\operatorname{KL}(P|Q)\ge0KL(P∣Q)≥0, with equality if and only if P=QP=QP=Q.

Proof

Write ϕ(s)=slog⁡s−s+1\phi(s)=s\log s-s+1ϕ(s)=slogs−s+1. Convexity gives ϕ(s)≥ϕ(1)+ϕ′(1)(s−1)=0\phi(s)\ge\phi(1)+\phi'(1)(s-1)=0ϕ(s)≥ϕ(1)+ϕ′(1)(s−1)=0, with equality only at s=1s=1s=1. Hence

KL⁡(P∣Q)=∑i,jQi,jϕ(Pi,j/Qi,j)≥0.\operatorname{KL}(P|Q) = \sum_{i,j}Q_{i,j}\phi(P_{i,j}/Q_{i,j}) \ge0.KL(P∣Q)=i,j∑​Qi,j​ϕ(Pi,j​/Qi,j​)≥0.
(14)
Proposition: Reference Measure Shift for KL

After removing zero-mass rows and columns, assume a,a′∈Δna,a'\in\simplex_na,a′∈Δn​ and b,b′∈Δmb,b'\in\simplex_mb,b′∈Δm​ have positive entries. For every P∈U(a,b)P\in\mathbf U(a,b)P∈U(a,b),

KL⁡(P∣a⊗b)=KL⁡(P∣a′⊗b′)−KL⁡(a∣a′)−KL⁡(b∣b′).\operatorname{KL}(P|a\otimes b) = \operatorname{KL}(P|a'\otimes b') - \operatorname{KL}(a|a') - \operatorname{KL}(b|b').KL(P∣a⊗b)=KL(P∣a′⊗b′)−KL(a∣a′)−KL(b∣b′).
(15)

Consequently, for fixed positive marginals, changing the positive tensor-product reference only adds a constant on the transport polytope.

Proof

Expand the logarithm and use the marginal constraints:

KL⁡(P∣a⊗b)=KL⁡(P∣a′⊗b′)+∑iailog⁡ai′ai+∑jbjlog⁡bj′bj=KL⁡(P∣a′⊗b′)−KL⁡(a∣a′)−KL⁡(b∣b′).\begin{aligned} \operatorname{KL}(P|a\otimes b) &= \operatorname{KL}(P|a'\otimes b') + \sum_i a_i\log\frac{a_i'}{a_i} + \sum_j b_j\log\frac{b_j'}{b_j} \\ &= \operatorname{KL}(P|a'\otimes b') - \operatorname{KL}(a|a') - \operatorname{KL}(b|b'). \end{aligned}KL(P∣a⊗b)​=KL(P∣a′⊗b′)+i∑​ai​logai​ai′​​+j∑​bj​logbj​bj′​​=KL(P∣a′⊗b′)−KL(a∣a′)−KL(b∣b′).​
(16)

The tensor-product reference is nevertheless useful when supports vary. It makes explicit which entries may vanish and passes cleanly to the continuous formulation.

Proposition: Convergence with ϵ\epsilonϵ

Assume, after removing zero-mass rows and columns, that aaa and bbb are positive and that CCC is finite. The unique solution PϵP_\epsilonPϵ​ converges, as ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0, to the maximum-entropy solution among all optimal solutions of the Kantorovich problem. Moreover,

Pϵ→a⊗bas ϵ→+∞.P_\epsilon \to a\otimes b \qquad \text{as } \epsilon\to+\infty.Pϵ​→a⊗bas ϵ→+∞.
(17)
Proof Sketch

For ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0, use compactness of the transport polytope and compare the optimality inequalities for the entropic problem against an exact Kantorovich optimizer. The cost gap is bounded by ϵ\epsilonϵ times a KL difference, so every cluster point is cost-optimal; after dividing by ϵ\epsilonϵ, the cluster point is the KL-minimizer on the optimal face.

For ϵ→+∞\epsilon\to+\inftyϵ→+∞, subtract a constant from CCC so that C≥0C\ge0C≥0. Testing the objective at a⊗ba\otimes ba⊗b gives

KL⁡(Pϵ∣a⊗b)≤⟨C,a⊗b⟩ϵ,\operatorname{KL}(P_\epsilon|a\otimes b) \le \frac{\langle C,a\otimes b\rangle}{\epsilon},KL(Pϵ​∣a⊗b)≤ϵ⟨C,a⊗b⟩​,
(18)

so the KL divergence to a⊗ba\otimes ba⊗b vanishes.

General Formulation¶

The continuous formulation replaces matrices by measures and discrete KL by relative entropy. This section records the measure-theoretic problem, explains how the temperature ϵ\epsilonϵ connects exact transport to the independent product coupling, and states the two asymptotic regimes that are useful later: a large-temperature expansion around independence and a small-temperature expansion around quadratic optimal transport.

Measure Formulation¶

The only structural change from the discrete problem is that matrix entries are replaced by densities with respect to a product reference measure. For probability measures α\alphaα and β\betaβ, define

Lcϵ(α,β):=min⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫X×Yc(x,y)  dπ(x,y)+ϵKL⁡(π∣α⊗β).\mathcal{L}_{c}^{\epsilon}(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \min_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int_{\X\times\Y}c(x,y)\,\d\pi(x,y) + \epsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi|\alpha\otimes\beta).Lcϵ​(α,β):=π∈Π(α,β)min​∫X×Y​c(x,y)dπ(x,y)+ϵKL(π∣α⊗β).
(19)
Definition: Relative Entropy of Measures

For nonnegative measures π\piπ and ξ\xiξ on X×Y\X\times\YX×Y,

KL⁡(π∣ξ):=∫X×Ylog⁡( dπ dξ(x,y)) dπ(x,y)+∫X×Y( dξ− dπ).\operatorname{KL}(\pi|\xi) \eqdef \int_{\X\times\Y} \log\left(\frac{\d\pi}{\d\xi}(x,y)\right)\d\pi(x,y) + \int_{\X\times\Y}(\d\xi-\d\pi).KL(π∣ξ):=∫X×Y​log(dξdπ​(x,y))dπ(x,y)+∫X×Y​(dξ−dπ).
(20)

By convention, KL⁡(π∣ξ)=+∞\operatorname{KL}(\pi|\xi)=+\inftyKL(π∣ξ)=+∞ if π\piπ is not absolutely continuous with respect to ξ\xiξ.

For fixed balanced marginals, the specific product reference only matters up to additive constants, provided the reference marginals are mutually absolutely continuous with α\alphaα and β\betaβ. Its support still matters: it determines which couplings have finite entropy.

Probabilistic Interpretation¶

Definition: Mutual Information

If (X,Y)∼π(X,Y)\sim\pi(X,Y)∼π have marginals X∼αX\sim\alphaX∼α and Y∼βY\sim\betaY∼β, their mutual information is

I(X,Y):=KL⁡(π∣α⊗β).\mathcal I(X,Y) \eqdef \operatorname{KL}(\pi|\alpha\otimes\beta).I(X,Y):=KL(π∣α⊗β).
(21)

It is nonnegative and vanishes if and only if XXX and YYY are independent.

With this terminology, the entropic problem is

inf⁡X∼α,  Y∼βE(c(X,Y))+ϵI(X,Y).\inf_{X\sim\alpha,\;Y\sim\beta} \mathbb E(c(X,Y))+\epsilon\mathcal I(X,Y).X∼α,Y∼βinf​E(c(X,Y))+ϵI(X,Y).
(22)

Large ϵ\epsilonϵ favors nearly independent endpoints, while small ϵ\epsilonϵ suppresses endpoint randomness and recovers an optimal Monge--Kantorovich coupling in the limit. When the unregularized quadratic problem has a Brenier map, this limiting coupling is deterministic.

Convergence with ϵ\epsilonϵ¶

The continuous problem has the same qualitative temperature limits as the finite-dimensional problem, but the zero-temperature selection is subtler. For quadratic transport between smooth densities, the limiting OT plan is typically supported on a graph and is therefore singular with respect to α⊗β\alpha\otimes\betaα⊗β. Thus the robust statement is weak convergence of minimizers. This is the standard Γ\GammaΓ-convergence mechanism for entropic OT Léonard, 2012Carlier et al., 2017; the density hypothesis below isolates the only approximation point needed in the proof.

Proposition: Convergence with ϵ\epsilonϵ for measures

Let X\XX and Y\YY be compact metric spaces, let c∈C(X×Y)c\in C(\X\times\Y)c∈C(X×Y), and let α∈P(X)\alpha\in\mathcal P(\X)α∈P(X) and β∈P(Y)\beta\in\mathcal P(\Y)β∈P(Y). Assume that finite-entropy couplings are dense in Π(α,β)\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)Π(α,β) for weak convergence with convergence of the cost integral. If πϵ\pi_\epsilonπϵ​ minimizes (19), then

Small-Temperature Expansion for Smooth Densities¶

At small temperature, entropic transport is a viscous perturbation of quadratic optimal transport. The expansion contains an ϵlog⁡ϵ\epsilon\log\epsilonϵlogϵ term from the Gaussian normalization of Brownian bridges, an endpoint entropy correction, and a Fisher-information term along the McCann interpolation. The formula below translates the small-noise Schrödinger expansion to the convention ∥x−y∥2+ϵKL⁡(⋅∣α⊗β)\|x-y\|^2+\epsilon\operatorname{KL}(\cdot|\alpha\otimes\beta)∥x−y∥2+ϵKL(⋅∣α⊗β) Conforti & Tamanini, 2021Chizat et al., 2020.

I0(α,β)=∫01∫Ω∥∇log⁡ρt(x)∥2ρt(x)  dx  dt<+∞.\mathcal I_0(\alpha,\beta) = \int_0^1\int_\Omega \|\nabla\log\rho_t(x)\|^2\rho_t(x)\,\d x\,\d t <+\infty.I0​(α,β)=∫01​∫Ω​∥∇logρt​(x)∥2ρt​(x)dxdt<+∞.

locally uniformly. The order-ϵ\epsilonϵ correction to the potentials is given by the Laplace prefactor in the soft ccc-transform equations, and depends on the endpoint densities and on the Hessian of the quadratic contact phase.

Dual of Sinkhorn¶

The dual point of view replaces couplings by potentials and soft ccc-transforms. It is the right formulation for stabilized implementations and differentiation.

Discrete Dual¶

The KL-normalized problem has the dual

min⁡P∈U(a,b)⟨P,C⟩+ϵKL⁡(P∣a⊗b)=max⁡f,g[⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩−ϵ∑i,jexp⁡(fi+gj−Ci,jϵ)aibj+ϵ].\min_{P\in\mathbf U(a,b)} \langle P,C\rangle+\epsilon\operatorname{KL}(P|a\otimes b) = \max_{f,g} \left[ \langle f,a\rangle+\langle g,b\rangle - \epsilon\sum_{i,j} \exp\left(\frac{f_i+g_j-C_{i,j}}{\epsilon}\right)a_i b_j + \epsilon \right].P∈U(a,b)min​⟨P,C⟩+ϵKL(P∣a⊗b)=f,gmax​[⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩−ϵi,j∑​exp(ϵfi​+gj​−Ci,j​​)ai​bj​+ϵ].
(34)

The optimal potentials are linked to the scaling variables through

ui=aiefi/ϵ,vj=bjegj/ϵ.u_i=a_i e^{f_i/\epsilon}, \qquad v_j=b_j e^{g_j/\epsilon}.ui​=ai​efi​/ϵ,vj​=bj​egj​/ϵ.
(35)

Discrete Soft ccc-Transforms¶

For fixed ggg, maximizing the dual with respect to fff gives

fi=−ϵlog⁡∑jexp⁡(gj−Ci,jϵ)bj.f_i = -\epsilon\log \sum_j \exp\left(\frac{g_j-C_{i,j}}{\epsilon}\right)b_j.fi​=−ϵlogj∑​exp(ϵgj​−Ci,j​​)bj​.
(36)

This is a smoothed minimum.

Definition: Soft-Min and Discrete Soft ccc-Transform

For h∈Rmh\in\RR^mh∈Rm and weights b∈Δmb\in\simplex_mb∈Δm​,

min⁡bϵ(h):=−ϵlog⁡∑je−hj/ϵbj.\min_b^\epsilon(h) \eqdef -\epsilon\log\sum_j e^{-h_j/\epsilon}b_j.bminϵ​(h):=−ϵlogj∑​e−hj​/ϵbj​.
(37)

It converges to min⁡jhj\min_j h_jminj​hj​ as ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0. Given a cost matrix CCC, the discrete soft ccc-transforms are

fi=min⁡bϵ(Ci,⋅−g),gj=min⁡aϵ(C⋅,j−f).f_i=\min_b^\epsilon(C_{i,\cdot}-g), \qquad g_j=\min_a^\epsilon(C_{\cdot,j}-f).fi​=bminϵ​(Ci,⋅​−g),gj​=aminϵ​(C⋅,j​−f).
(38)

Exponentiating the alternating soft-transform iterations recovers Sinkhorn’s algorithm. For small ϵ\epsilonϵ, one must compute the log-sum-exp terms with the usual stabilization trick: subtract the minimum before exponentiating and add it back afterward.

For compact spaces and continuous cost, the KL-regularized problem has the concave dual

Dϵ(f,g)=∫f  dα+∫g  dβ−ϵ∫(e(f(x)+g(y)−c(x,y))/ϵ−1) dα(x) dβ(y).\mathcal D_\epsilon(f,g) = \int f\,\d\alpha+\int g\,\d\beta - \epsilon \int \left( e^{(f(x)+g(y)-c(x,y))/\epsilon} - 1 \right) \d\alpha(x)\d\beta(y).Dϵ​(f,g)=∫fdα+∫gdβ−ϵ∫(e(f(x)+g(y)−c(x,y))/ϵ−1)dα(x)dβ(y).

This is the smooth counterpart of the hard feasibility constraint f⊕g≤cf\oplus g\le cf⊕g≤c from the Kantorovich dual.

Definition: Continuous Soft ccc-Transforms

For f∈C(X)f\in\Cc(\X)f∈C(X) and g∈C(Y)g\in\Cc(\Y)g∈C(Y),

fc,ϵ(y):=−ϵlog⁡∫Xe(f(x)−c(x,y))/ϵ dα(x),f^{c,\epsilon}(y) \eqdef -\epsilon\log \int_\X e^{(f(x)-c(x,y))/\epsilon} \d\alpha(x),fc,ϵ(y):=−ϵlog∫X​e(f(x)−c(x,y))/ϵdα(x),

gcˉ,ϵ(x):=−ϵlog⁡∫Ye(g(y)−c(x,y))/ϵ dβ(y).g^{\bar c,\epsilon}(x) \eqdef -\epsilon\log \int_\Y e^{(g(y)-c(x,y))/\epsilon} \d\beta(y).gcˉ,ϵ(x):=−ϵlog∫Y​e(g(y)−c(x,y))/ϵdβ(y).
(42)
Proposition: Existence and Uniqueness of Entropic Dual Potentials

Assume X\XX and Y\YY are compact and ccc is continuous. The dual problem has solutions, and the set of solutions is

(f⋆+λ,g⋆−λ),λ∈R.(f^\star+\lambda,g^\star-\lambda), \qquad \lambda\in\RR .(f⋆+λ,g⋆−λ),λ∈R.
(43)
Proof Sketch

Normalize potentials by imposing ∫f  dα=0\int f\,\d\alpha=0∫fdα=0. Replacing a pair of potentials by the corresponding soft transforms does not decrease the dual objective. The transformed potentials have oscillations bounded by the oscillation of ccc, and their modulus of continuity is controlled by the modulus of continuity of ccc. Arzela--Ascoli gives existence.

Uniqueness up to constants follows from strict convexity of H↦∫eH/ϵ d(α⊗β)H\mapsto\int e^{H/\epsilon}\d(\alpha\otimes\beta)H↦∫eH/ϵd(α⊗β) on the image of (f,g)↦f⊕g−c(f,g)\mapsto f\oplus g-c(f,g)↦f⊕g−c, modulo constants.

Remark: Convexity properties of soft transforms

The log-sum-exp part behaves like a smoothed maximum and preserves convexity. Since the soft transform takes the negative of this quantity after inserting the cost, it preserves the usual ccc-concavity structure. In particular, for the bilinear cost c(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩c(x,y)=-\dotp{x}{y}c(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩, the transform fc,ϵf^{c,\epsilon}fc,ϵ is concave for any fff. Therefore, for the quadratic cost c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2/2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2/2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2/2, the optimal potentials have the form f⋆(x)=∥x∥2/2−ϕ⋆(x)f^\star(x)=\norm{x}^2/2-\phi^\star(x)f⋆(x)=∥x∥2/2−ϕ⋆(x) and g⋆(y)=∥y∥2/2−ψ⋆(y)g^\star(y)=\norm{y}^2/2-\psi^\star(y)g⋆(y)=∥y∥2/2−ψ⋆(y), where ϕ⋆\phi^\starϕ⋆ and ψ⋆\psi^\starψ⋆ are convex.

Neural Dual Solvers¶

The convex-potential structure above suggests a sample-based alternative to evaluating soft transforms on a grid or on all pairs of samples. For the bilinear cost c(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩c(x,y)=-\dotp{x}{y}c(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩, the signs of the dual potentials are convex: writing Φ=−f\Phi=-fΦ=−f and Ψ=−g\Psi=-gΨ=−g, the zero-temperature constraint f(x)+g(y)≤−⟨x,y⟩f(x)+g(y)\leq-\dotp{x}{y}f(x)+g(y)≤−⟨x,y⟩ becomes

Φ(x)+Ψ(y)≥⟨x,y⟩.\Phi(x)+\Psi(y)\geq \dotp{x}{y}.Φ(x)+Ψ(y)≥⟨x,y⟩.
(44)

For the quadratic cost this is the same statement after subtracting the quadratic terms. One can therefore maximize the continuous dual over parameterized convex potentials, estimating the integrals by stochastic samples.

A useful parameterization is given by input-convex neural networks (ICNNs) Amos et al., 2017Makkuva et al., 2020. The construction mirrors elementary closure rules for convex functions: nonnegative linear combinations preserve convexity, composition with a convex nondecreasing scalar nonlinearity preserves convexity, and the ReLU r↦max⁡(r,0)r\mapsto\max(r,0)r↦max(r,0) is both convex and nondecreasing. Thus a feed-forward network with nonnegative hidden-to-hidden weights and affine skip connections from the input defines a convex function of its input. This gives a flexible cone of convex trial potentials, although the finite-dimensional optimization over the network weights is not a convex optimization problem. Universal-approximation statements must be read with this distinction in mind: max-affine functions are dense among continuous convex functions on compact convex sets, and ICNN-type architectures are designed to inherit this approximation principle. General ReLU universal approximation results, such as the width d+1d+1d+1 theorem on compact subsets of Rd\RR^dRd Hanin, 2019, provide useful background but do not by themselves enforce convexity. In practice, neural dual solvers trade exact Sinkhorn scaling for amortized stochastic optimization of the dual potentials.

Remark: Gaussian marginals

For c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2 and Gaussian marginals, the soft transforms preserve quadratic functions, because products and convolutions of Gaussian functions remain Gaussian. Hence optimal entropic potentials are quadratic and the optimal entropic coupling is Gaussian. Section Entropic Optimal Transport Between Gaussians makes this finite-dimensional closure explicit.

Algorithm: Log-domain Sinkhorn by soft transforms

Output: Entropic coupling P\PP computed from stabilized potentials.

While ηk>tol\eta_k>\mathrm{tol}ηk​>tol do:

Set k←k+1k\leftarrow k+1k←k+1.

Compute stabilized soft transform: fi(k)=−ϵlog⁡∑jexp⁡ ⁣(gj(k−1)−Cijϵ)bj.\fD_i^{(k)} = -\epsilon\log\sum_j \exp\!\left(\frac{\gD_j^{(k-1)}-\C_{ij}}{\epsilon}\right)\b_j.fi(k)​=−ϵlog∑j​exp(ϵgj(k−1)​−Cij​​)bj​.

Compute stabilized reverse soft transform: gj(k)=−ϵlog⁡∑iexp⁡ ⁣(fi(k)−Cijϵ)ai.\gD_j^{(k)} = -\epsilon\log\sum_i \exp\!\left(\frac{\fD_i^{(k)}-\C_{ij}}{\epsilon}\right)\a_i.gj(k)​=−ϵlog∑i​exp(ϵfi(k)​−Cij​​)ai​.

Set ηk=max⁡{∥f(k)−f(k−1)∥∞,∥g(k)−g(k−1)∥∞}\eta_k=\max\{\norm{\fD^{(k)}-\fD^{(k-1)}}_\infty,\norm{\gD^{(k)}-\gD^{(k-1)}}_\infty\}ηk​=max{∥∥​f(k)−f(k−1)∥∥​∞​,∥∥​g(k)−g(k−1)∥∥​∞​}, with the first term ignored for k=1k=1k=1.

Return Pij=aibjexp⁡ ⁣(fi(k)+gj(k)−Cijϵ).\P_{ij} = \a_i\b_j \exp\!\left(\frac{\fD_i^{(k)}+\gD_j^{(k)}-\C_{ij}}{\epsilon}\right).Pij​=ai​bj​exp(ϵfi(k)​+gj(k)​−Cij​​).

The path-space meaning of the static Schrodinger problem now follows the dual construction. A noisy reference dynamics first defines a probability law on trajectories; after optimizing out the conditional law of the path given its endpoints, only the endpoint coupling remains.

Path-Space Schrodinger Problem¶

Schrodinger’s reciprocal problem is naturally posed on paths rather than on endpoint pairs. The Sinkhorn problem appears after the path law is reduced to its two endpoint marginals.

Unregularized Path-Space Transport¶

Let Ω=C([0,1];X)\Omega=C([0,1];\X)Ω=C([0,1];X) be a path space and let et(ω)=ωte_t(\omega)=\omega_tet​(ω)=ωt​ be the evaluation maps. Given a path action A:Ω→[0,+∞]\mathcal A:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]A:Ω→[0,+∞], the unregularized path-space problem is

inf⁡M∈P(Ω){∫ΩA(ω)  dM(ω):(e0)♯M=α, (e1)♯M=β}.\inf_{M\in\mathcal P(\Omega)} \left\{ \int_\Omega\mathcal A(\omega)\,\d M(\omega) : (e_0)_\sharp M=\alpha,\ (e_1)_\sharp M=\beta \right\}.M∈P(Ω)inf​{∫Ω​A(ω)dM(ω):(e0​)♯​M=α, (e1​)♯​M=β}.
(45)

A(ω)={∫01∥ω˙t∥2  dt,ω absolutely continuous,+∞,otherwise.\mathcal A(\omega) = \begin{cases} \int_0^1\norm{\dot\omega_t}^2\,\d t, & \omega\text{ absolutely continuous},\\ +\infty, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}A(ω)={∫01​∥ω˙t​∥2dt,+∞,​ω absolutely continuous,otherwise.​

Conversely, mix selected minimizing paths according to any coupling π\piπ and then optimize over π\piπ.

Entropic Path-Space Problem¶

Let Rϵ∈P(Ω)R^\epsilon\in\mathcal P(\Omega)Rϵ∈P(Ω) be a reference path law, for instance a Brownian or Langevin dynamics at noise level ϵ\epsilonϵ. The dynamic Schrodinger bridge problem is the entropy projection

SBϵ(α,β):=inf⁡M∈P(Ω){ϵKL⁡(M∣Rϵ):(e0)♯M=α, (e1)♯M=β}.\mathrm{SB}_\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \inf_{M\in\mathcal P(\Omega)} \left\{ \epsilon\operatorname{KL}(M|R^\epsilon): (e_0)_\sharp M=\alpha,\ (e_1)_\sharp M=\beta \right\}.SBϵ​(α,β):=M∈P(Ω)inf​{ϵKL(M∣Rϵ):(e0​)♯​M=α, (e1​)♯​M=β}.
(51)

It asks for the most likely path law, relative to the prior dynamics, among all path laws matching the observed endpoints Schrödinger, 1931Léonard, 2012Léonard, 2014Chen et al., 2016.

Stochastic-Control Interpretation¶

For Brownian references, the entropy projection has a direct control meaning. To fix constants, suppose that RϵR^\epsilonRϵ is the law of

 dXt=ϵ  dBt,X0∼α,\d X_t = \sqrt{\epsilon}\,\d B_t, \qquad X_0\sim\alpha ,dXt​=ϵ​dBt​,X0​∼α,
(52)

so that the generator is (ϵ/2)Δ(\epsilon/2)\Delta(ϵ/2)Δ. Under the standard finite-entropy assumptions, a path law MMM with the same initial marginal and M≪RϵM\ll R^\epsilonM≪Rϵ can be represented, in the weak sense, by an adapted drift utu_tut​ of finite energy,

 dXt=ut  dt+ϵ  dBt,X0∼α.\d X_t = u_t\,\d t+\sqrt{\epsilon}\,\d B_t, \qquad X_0\sim\alpha .dXt​=ut​dt+ϵ​dBt​,X0​∼α.
(53)

Conversely, such a drift defines an absolutely continuous change of law when the usual Girsanov integrability conditions hold. Girsanov’s formula then gives

KL⁡(M∣Rϵ)=12ϵEM∫01∥ut∥2  dt,ϵKL⁡(M∣Rϵ)=12EM∫01∥ut∥2  dt.\operatorname{KL}(M|R^\epsilon) = \frac{1}{2\epsilon}\mathbb E_M\int_0^1\norm{u_t}^2\,\d t, \qquad \epsilon\operatorname{KL}(M|R^\epsilon) = \frac12\mathbb E_M\int_0^1\norm{u_t}^2\,\d t .KL(M∣Rϵ)=2ϵ1​EM​∫01​∥ut​∥2dt,ϵKL(M∣Rϵ)=21​EM​∫01​∥ut​∥2dt.
(54)

If the reference initial law is not α\alphaα, an additional term ϵKL⁡(α∣R0ϵ)\epsilon\operatorname{KL}(\alpha|R^\epsilon_0)ϵKL(α∣R0ϵ​) appears, but it is fixed by the endpoint constraint. Hence, up to this fixed endpoint cost, the Schrodinger bridge can be read as

inf⁡u{12E∫01∥ut∥2  dt: dXt=ut  dt+ϵ  dBt,X0∼α, X1∼β}.\inf_u \left\{ \frac12\mathbb E\int_0^1\norm{u_t}^2\,\d t : \d X_t=u_t\,\d t+\sqrt{\epsilon}\,\d B_t,\quad X_0\sim\alpha,\ X_1\sim\beta \right\}.uinf​{21​E∫01​∥ut​∥2dt:dXt​=ut​dt+ϵ​dBt​,X0​∼α, X1​∼β}.
(55)

Thus the bridge is the least energetic change of drift that steers the Brownian prior from α\alphaα to β\betaβ. The optimizer may be chosen Markovian. If hth_tht​ denotes the positive space-time harmonic Schrodinger factor associated with the terminal constraint, then the optimal feedback drift has the Doob-transform form

ut⋆(x)=ϵ∇log⁡ht(x).u_t^\star(x)=\epsilon\nabla\log h_t(x).ut⋆​(x)=ϵ∇loght​(x).
(56)

Equivalently, with the value potential ϕt=ϵlog⁡ht\phi_t=\epsilon\log h_tϕt​=ϵloght​, one has ut⋆=∇ϕtu_t^\star=\nabla\phi_tut⋆​=∇ϕt​ and ϕt\phi_tϕt​ solves the viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equation ∂tϕt+12∥∇ϕt∥2+ϵ2Δϕt=0\partial_t\phi_t+\frac12\norm{\nabla\phi_t}^2+\frac{\epsilon}{2}\Delta\phi_t=0∂t​ϕt​+21​∥∇ϕt​∥2+2ϵ​Δϕt​=0. This control viewpoint and the endpoint-coupling reduction below are two faces of the same object: the controlled diffusion describes the whole path law, whereas the static Sinkhorn coupling records only its two endpoints.

Viscous Benamou--Brenier Formulations¶

The dynamic problem also has viscous Benamou--Brenier formulations. In one common convention,

∂tρt+div⁡(ρtvt)=σ2Δρt\partial_t\rho_t+\operatorname{div}(\rho_t v_t) = \frac{\sigma}{2}\Delta\rho_t∂t​ρt​+div(ρt​vt​)=2σ​Δρt​
(57)

and one minimizes a kinetic action. After absorbing the diffusion into the velocity ut=vt−σ2∇log⁡ρtu_t=v_t-\frac{\sigma}{2}\nabla\log\rho_tut​=vt​−2σ​∇logρt​, the same minimizers are obtained from

∫01 ⁣∫(12∥ut(x)∥2+σ28∥∇log⁡ρt(x)∥2)ρt(x)  dx  dt,\int_0^1\!\int \left( \frac12\norm{u_t(x)}^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{8}\norm{\nabla\log\rho_t(x)}^2 \right) \rho_t(x)\,\d x\,\d t,∫01​∫(21​∥ut​(x)∥2+8σ2​∥∇logρt​(x)∥2)ρt​(x)dxdt,
(58)

up to endpoint entropy terms. The extra term is a Fisher-information penalty.

Proposition: Endpoint Reduction of the Schrodinger Problem

Assume regular conditional laws exist and that the relative-entropy chain rule applies. If R01ϵ=(e0,e1)♯RϵR^\epsilon_{01}=(e_0,e_1)_\sharp R^\epsilonR01ϵ​=(e0​,e1​)♯​Rϵ, then

SBϵ(α,β)=inf⁡π∈Π(α,β)ϵKL⁡(π∣R01ϵ).\mathrm{SB}_\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) = \inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \epsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi|R^\epsilon_{01}).SBϵ​(α,β)=π∈Π(α,β)inf​ϵKL(π∣R01ϵ​).
(59)

For a fixed endpoint coupling π\piπ, the minimizing path law is the mixture of reference bridges

Mπ=∫Rϵ,x,y  dπ(x,y).M^\pi = \int R^{\epsilon,x,y}\,\d\pi(x,y).Mπ=∫Rϵ,x,ydπ(x,y).
(60)
Proof

Disintegrate both MMM and RϵR^\epsilonRϵ with respect to their endpoint pairs. The chain rule gives

KL⁡(M∣Rϵ)=KL⁡(π∣R01ϵ)+∫KL⁡(Mx,y∣Rϵ,x,y)  dπ(x,y).\operatorname{KL}(M|R^\epsilon) = \operatorname{KL}(\pi|R^\epsilon_{01}) + \int \operatorname{KL}(M^{x,y}|R^{\epsilon,x,y}) \,\d\pi(x,y).KL(M∣Rϵ)=KL(π∣R01ϵ​)+∫KL(Mx,y∣Rϵ,x,y)dπ(x,y).
(61)

The second term is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when the conditional path law is the reference bridge for π\piπ-almost every endpoint pair.

Brownian Bridges and Sinkhorn Couplings¶

For Brownian reference dynamics on Rd\RR^dRd, the endpoint prior has heat-kernel density proportional to

exp⁡(−∥x−y∥2ϵ).\exp\left(-\frac{\norm{x-y}^2}{\epsilon}\right).exp(−ϵ∥x−y∥2​).
(62)

After rewriting this prior with respect to α⊗β\alpha\otimes\betaα⊗β, the endpoint problem is exactly the continuous Sinkhorn problem up to an additive constant. Sinkhorn computes which endpoints should be paired; the path-space Schrodinger bridge then connects each pair by a Brownian bridge.

Algorithm: Endpoint-to-path Schr"odinger lift

Input: Endpoint laws α,β\alpha,\betaα,β, cost ccc, regularization ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, reference bridges Rϵ,x,y\Rr^{\epsilon,x,y}Rϵ,x,y.

Output: Schrodinger path law Mϵ⋆M_\epsilon^\starMϵ⋆​.

Let πϵ⋆\pi_\epsilon^\starπϵ⋆​ be a minimizer of the static entropic endpoint problem: πϵ⋆∈arg min⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫c  dπ+ϵKL⁡(π∣α⊗β).\pi_\epsilon^\star \in \argmin_{\pi\in\Couplings(\al,\be)} \int c\,\d\pi+\epsilon\KL(\pi|\al\otimes\be).πϵ⋆​∈argminπ∈Π(α,β)​∫cdπ+ϵKL(π∣α⊗β).

For each endpoint pair (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) sampled from πϵ⋆\pi_\epsilon^\starπϵ⋆​ do:

Draw bridge path: ω∼Rϵ,x,y.\omega\sim\Rr^{\epsilon,x,y}.ω∼Rϵ,x,y.

Return Mϵ⋆=∫Rϵ,x,y  dπϵ⋆(x,y).M_\epsilon^\star= \int \Rr^{\epsilon,x,y}\,\d\pi_\epsilon^\star(x,y).Mϵ⋆​=∫Rϵ,x,ydπϵ⋆​(x,y).

Marginal-Dependent Problems¶

The balanced Sinkhorn problem fixes both marginals exactly. Many nearby models instead optimize the transported marginals, but only through penalties or constraints applied separately to each marginal. The useful point, emphasized by the generalized scaling algorithms of Chizat, Peyré, Schmitzer and Vialard Chizat et al., 2018, is that entropic OT remains a diagonal-scaling problem whenever these marginal terms admit simple KL-proximal maps.

Let F\mathcal FF and G\mathcal GG be proper convex lower semicontinuous functionals on finite nonnegative measures on X\XxX and Y\YyY. The unregularized marginal-dependent transport problem is

inf⁡π∈M+(X×Y)∫c(x,y)  dπ(x,y)+F(π1)+G(π2),\inf_{\pi\in\Mm_+(\Xx\times\Yy)} \int c(x,y)\,\d\pi(x,y) + \mathcal F(\pi_1) + \mathcal G(\pi_2),π∈M+​(X×Y)inf​∫c(x,y)dπ(x,y)+F(π1​)+G(π2​),
(63)

where π1=(pX)♯π\pi_1=(\mathrm p_{\Xx})_\sharp\piπ1​=(pX​)♯​π and π2=(pY)♯π\pi_2=(\mathrm p_{\Yy})_\sharp\piπ2​=(pY​)♯​π are the two marginals of π\piπ. Entropic regularization turns this problem into the scaling-friendly form

inf⁡π∈M+(X×Y)∫c(x,y)  dπ(x,y)+F(π1)+G(π2)+ϵKL⁡(π∣α⊗β),\inf_{\pi\in\Mm_+(\Xx\times\Yy)} \int c(x,y)\,\d\pi(x,y) + \mathcal F(\pi_1) + \mathcal G(\pi_2) + \epsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi|\alpha\otimes\beta),π∈M+​(X×Y)inf​∫c(x,y)dπ(x,y)+F(π1​)+G(π2​)+ϵKL(π∣α⊗β),
(64)

where α\alphaα and β\betaβ are reference measures. In this subsection, when the total mass of π\piπ is not fixed, the KL term is understood in the generalized sense associated with φ(s)=slog⁡s−s+1\varphi(s)=s\log s-s+1φ(s)=slogs−s+1. Thus, if λ=α⊗β\lambda=\alpha\otimes\betaλ=α⊗β and π=ρλ+π⊥\pi=\rho\lambda+\pi^\perpπ=ρλ+π⊥ is the Lebesgue decomposition of π\piπ with respect to λ\lambdaλ, then

KL⁡(π∣λ)=∫(ρlog⁡ρ−ρ+1) dλ\operatorname{KL}(\pi|\lambda) = \int \bigl(\rho\log\rho-\rho+1\bigr)\,\mathrm d\lambdaKL(π∣λ)=∫(ρlogρ−ρ+1)dλ
(65)

with value +∞+\infty+∞ when π⊥≠0\pi^\perp\ne0π⊥=0. On probability couplings this coincides with the usual relative entropy.

Balanced OT is recovered by taking F=ι{α}\mathcal F=\iota_{\{\alpha\}}F=ι{α}​ and G=ι{β}\mathcal G=\iota_{\{\beta\}}G=ι{β}​. Unbalanced OT replaces these hard indicators by marginal divergences, as developed later in Section Unbalanced OT. An entropic JKO step fixes the first marginal to the previous iterate and puts the energy on the second marginal, for instance F=ι{αt}\mathcal F=\iota_{\{\alpha_t\}}F=ι{αt​}​ and G=E\mathcal G=EG=E, with cost c/(2τ)c/(2\tau)c/(2τ); this is the static counterpart of the minimizing-movement schemes of Chapter Paragraph. Barycenters are the multi-coupling extension: several couplings share one unknown marginal and are treated by the generalized Sinkhorn updates of Section OT Barycenters.

In finite dimension, with reference weights satisfying ai,bj>0a_i,b_j>0ai​,bj​>0 and proper convex functions F:R+n→R∪{+∞}\mathsf F:\RR_+^n\to\RR\cup\{+\infty\}F:R+n​→R∪{+∞}, G:R+m→R∪{+∞}\mathsf G:\RR_+^m\to\RR\cup\{+\infty\}G:R+m​→R∪{+∞}, the entropic version becomes

inf⁡P∈R+n×m⟨C,P⟩+F(P1m)+G(P⊤1n)+ϵKL(P∣a⊗b).\inf_{\P\in\RR_+^{n\times m}} \langle\C,\P\rangle + \mathsf F(\P\ones_m) + \mathsf G(\P^\top\ones_n) + \epsilon\KLD(\P|\a\otimes\b).P∈R+n×m​inf​⟨C,P⟩+F(P1m​)+G(P⊤1n​)+ϵKL(P∣a⊗b).
(66)

Equivalently, if Kij=aibje−Cij/ϵ\K_{ij}=a_i b_j e^{-\C_{ij}/\epsilon}Kij​=ai​bj​e−Cij​/ϵ, the terms involving C\CC can be absorbed into the Gibbs reference and the problem is, up to the additive constant ϵ∑i,j(aibj−Kij)\epsilon\sum_{i,j}(a_i b_j-\K_{ij})ϵ∑i,j​(ai​bj​−Kij​),

inf⁡P≥0F(P1m)+G(P⊤1n)+ϵKL(P∣K).\inf_{\P\ge0} \mathsf F(\P\ones_m) + \mathsf G(\P^\top\ones_n) + \epsilon\KLD(\P|\K).P≥0inf​F(P1m​)+G(P⊤1n​)+ϵKL(P∣K).
(67)
Proposition: Dual and scaling for marginal penalties

Assume ai,bj>0a_i,b_j>0ai​,bj​>0, ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, and a Fenchel qualification condition, for instance the existence of a matrix P>0\P>0P>0 such that P1m\P\ones_mP1m​ and P⊤1n\P^\top\ones_nP⊤1n​ belong to the relative interiors of dom⁡(F)\operatorname{dom}(\mathsf F)dom(F) and dom⁡(G)\operatorname{dom}(\mathsf G)dom(G). The Fenchel dual of the discrete marginal-dependent problem is

sup⁡f∈Rn,g∈Rm−F∗(−f)−G∗(−g)−ϵ∑i,jaibj[exp⁡(fi+gj−Cijϵ)−1].\sup_{\mathbf f\in\RR^n,\mathbf g\in\RR^m} - \mathsf F^*(-\mathbf f) - \mathsf G^*(-\mathbf g) - \epsilon\sum_{i,j}a_i b_j \left[ \exp\left(\frac{\mathbf f_i+\mathbf g_j-\C_{ij}}{\epsilon}\right)-1 \right].f∈Rn,g∈Rmsup​−F∗(−f)−G∗(−g)−ϵi,j∑​ai​bj​[exp(ϵfi​+gj​−Cij​​)−1].
(68)

Equivalently, up to the additive constant ϵ∑i,jaibj\epsilon\sum_{i,j}a_i b_jϵ∑i,j​ai​bj​, the last term is

−ϵ∑i,jKijexp⁡(fi+gjϵ).- \epsilon\sum_{i,j}\K_{ij} \exp\left(\frac{\mathbf f_i+\mathbf g_j}{\epsilon}\right).−ϵi,j∑​Kij​exp(ϵfi​+gj​​).

If u=ef/ϵ\mathbf u=e^{\mathbf f/\epsilon}u=ef/ϵ and v=eg/ϵ\mathbf v=e^{\mathbf g/\epsilon}v=eg/ϵ, exact block ascent in the two dual variables is the generalized Sinkhorn cycle

r←prox⁡F/ϵKL(Kv),u←r⊘(Kv),s←prox⁡G/ϵKL(K⊤u),v←s⊘(K⊤u),P=diag⁡(u)Kdiag⁡(v),\begin{aligned} r &\leftarrow \operatorname{prox}_{\mathsf F/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(\K\mathbf v), &\qquad \mathbf u &\leftarrow r\oslash(\K\mathbf v),\\ s &\leftarrow \operatorname{prox}_{\mathsf G/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(\K^\top\mathbf u), &\qquad \mathbf v &\leftarrow s\oslash(\K^\top\mathbf u),\\ \P&=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf u)\K\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf v), \end{aligned}rsP​←proxF/ϵKL​(Kv),←proxG/ϵKL​(K⊤u),=diag(u)Kdiag(v),​uv​←r⊘(Kv),←s⊘(K⊤u),​
(70)

where divisions are entrywise and

prox⁡hKL(z):=arg min⁡r∈R+dh(r)+KL(r∣z).\operatorname{prox}^{\KLD}_{\mathsf h}(z) \eqdef \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{r\in\RR_+^d} \mathsf h(r)+\KLD(r|z).proxhKL​(z):=r∈R+d​argmin​h(r)+KL(r∣z).
(71)

In particular, prox⁡F/ϵKL(z)\operatorname{prox}_{\mathsf F/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(z)proxF/ϵKL​(z) is the minimizer of F(r)+ϵKL(r∣z)\mathsf F(r)+\epsilon\KLD(r|z)F(r)+ϵKL(r∣z).

Proof

Introduce independent variables rrr and sss for the two marginals and use dual variables f,g\mathbf f,\mathbf gf,g for the constraints r=P1mr=\P\ones_mr=P1m​ and s=P⊤1ns=\P^\top\ones_ns=P⊤1n​. The Lagrangian contains

F(r)+⟨f,r⟩+G(s)+⟨g,s⟩+⟨C,P⟩+ϵKL(P∣a⊗b)−⟨f⊕g,P⟩.\mathsf F(r)+\langle\mathbf f,r\rangle + \mathsf G(s)+\langle\mathbf g,s\rangle + \langle\C,\P\rangle + \epsilon\KLD(\P|\a\otimes\b) - \langle\mathbf f\oplus\mathbf g,\P\rangle.F(r)+⟨f,r⟩+G(s)+⟨g,s⟩+⟨C,P⟩+ϵKL(P∣a⊗b)−⟨f⊕g,P⟩.

Minimizing over rrr and sss gives −F∗(−f)-\mathsf F^*(-\mathbf f)−F∗(−f) and −G∗(−g)-\mathsf G^*(-\mathbf g)−G∗(−g). For each scalar entry, the convex conjugate of p↦Cijp+ϵ(plog⁡(p/(aibj))−p+aibj)p\mapsto C_{ij}p+\epsilon(p\log(p/(a_i b_j))-p+a_i b_j)p↦Cij​p+ϵ(plog(p/(ai​bj​))−p+ai​bj​) is q↦ϵaibj(e(q−Cij)/ϵ−1)q\mapsto\epsilon a_i b_j(e^{(q-C_{ij})/\epsilon}-1)q↦ϵai​bj​(e(q−Cij​)/ϵ−1). For the scaling form, fix v>0\mathbf v>0v>0, set K~=Kdiag⁡(v)\widetilde{\K}=\K\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf v)K=Kdiag(v) and z=K~1m=Kvz=\widetilde{\K}\ones_m=\K\mathbf vz=K1m​=Kv. Updating the row scaling means looking for P=diag⁡(u)K~\P=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf u)\widetilde{\K}P=diag(u)K, so its row marginal is r=P1m=u⊙zr=\P\ones_m=\mathbf u\odot zr=P1m​=u⊙z. Thus exact optimization of this block is equivalent to minimizing F(r)+ϵKL(r∣z)\mathsf F(r)+\epsilon\KLD(r|z)F(r)+ϵKL(r∣z) over r≥0r\ge0r≥0, hence r=prox⁡F/ϵKL(z)r=\operatorname{prox}_{\mathsf F/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(z)r=proxF/ϵKL​(z) and u=r⊘z\mathbf u=r\oslash zu=r⊘z. The column update is identical with w=K⊤uw=\K^\top\mathbf uw=K⊤u.

When F=ι{a}\mathsf F=\iota_{\{\a\}}F=ι{a}​ and G=ι{b}\mathsf G=\iota_{\{\b\}}G=ι{b}​, the first two dual terms are ⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩\langle\mathbf f,\a\rangle+\langle\mathbf g,\b\rangle⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩, and one recovers the usual entropic dual. The classical Sinkhorn update is the special case in which the KL proximal maps return the prescribed marginals a\aa and b\bb.

Algorithm: Generalized Sinkhorn for marginal penalties

Input: Reference weights a,b\a,\ba,b, cost C\CC, convex marginal penalties F,G\mathsf F,\mathsf GF,G, regularization ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, tolerance tol\mathrm{tol}tol.

Output: Coupling P\PP and optimized marginals r=P1mr=\P\ones_mr=P1m​, s=P⊤1ns=\transp{\P}\ones_ns=P⊤1n​.

Set Kij=aibje−Cij/ϵ\K_{ij}=a_i b_j e^{-\C_{ij}/\epsilon}Kij​=ai​bj​e−Cij​/ϵ.

Initialize: u=1n\uD=\ones_nu=1n​, v=1m\vD=\ones_mv=1m​, η=+∞\eta=+\inftyη=+∞.

While η>tol\eta>\mathrm{tol}η>tol do:

Store uold=u\uD_{\mathrm{old}}=\uDuold​=u and vold=v\vD_{\mathrm{old}}=\vDvold​=v.

Set z=Kvz=\K\vDz=Kv.

Compute r=prox⁡F/ϵKL(z)r=\prox_{\mathsf F/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(z)r=proxF/ϵKL​(z).

Set u=r⊘z\uD=r\oslash zu=r⊘z.

Set w=K⊤uw=\transp{\K}\uDw=K⊤u.

Compute s=prox⁡G/ϵKL(w)s=\prox_{\mathsf G/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(w)s=proxG/ϵKL​(w).

Set v=s⊘w\vD=s\oslash wv=s⊘w.

Set η=max⁡{∥u−uold∥∞,∥v−vold∥∞}\eta=\max\{\norm{\uD-\uD_{\mathrm{old}}}_\infty,\norm{\vD-\vD_{\mathrm{old}}}_\infty\}η=max{∥u−uold​∥∞​,∥v−vold​∥∞​}.

Return P=diag⁡(u)Kdiag⁡(v)\P=\diag(\uD)\K\diag(\vD)P=diag(u)Kdiag(v), r=P1mr=\P\ones_mr=P1m​, and s=P⊤1ns=\transp{\P}\ones_ns=P⊤1n​.

The usefulness of this formulation is that many KL-proximal maps are explicit.

  • Hard marginal constraint. If F=ι{a}\mathsf F=\iota_{\{\a\}}F=ι{a}​, then prox⁡F/ϵKL(z)=a\operatorname{prox}_{\mathsf F/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(z)=\aproxF/ϵKL​(z)=a.

  • KL marginal relaxation. If F(r)=τKL(r∣a)\mathsf F(r)=\tau\KLD(r|\a)F(r)=τKL(r∣a) with τ>0\tau>0τ>0, then, coordinatewise,

prox⁡F/ϵKL(z)=zϵ/(τ+ϵ)⊙aτ/(τ+ϵ),\operatorname{prox}_{\mathsf F/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(z) = z^{\epsilon/(\tau+\epsilon)}\odot \a^{\tau/(\tau+\epsilon)},proxF/ϵKL​(z)=zϵ/(τ+ϵ)⊙aτ/(τ+ϵ),
(74)

so u←(a⊘z)τ/(τ+ϵ)\mathbf u\leftarrow(\a\oslash z)^{\tau/(\tau+\epsilon)}u←(a⊘z)τ/(τ+ϵ), the damped scaling of unbalanced Sinkhorn.

  • Pointwise bounds. If F=ι{ℓ≤r≤u}\mathsf F=\iota_{\{\ell\le r\le u\}}F=ι{ℓ≤r≤u}​, then the proximal map is the coordinatewise clipping prox⁡F/ϵKL(z)i=min⁡{ui,max⁡{ℓi,zi}}\operatorname{prox}_{\mathsf F/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(z)_i=\min\{u_i,\max\{\ell_i,z_i\}\}proxF/ϵKL​(z)i​=min{ui​,max{ℓi​,zi​}}.

  • Total-variation marginal relaxation. If F(r)=τ∥r−a∥1\mathsf F(r)=\tau\norm{r-\a}_1F(r)=τ∥r−a∥1​ and λ=τ/ϵ\lambda=\tau/\epsilonλ=τ/ϵ, then

prox⁡F/ϵKL(z)i={zieλ,zi<aie−λ,ai,aie−λ≤zi≤aieλ,zie−λ,zi>aieλ.\operatorname{prox}_{\mathsf F/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(z)_i = \begin{cases} z_i e^{\lambda}, & z_i<a_i e^{-\lambda},\\ a_i, & a_i e^{-\lambda}\le z_i\le a_i e^{\lambda},\\ z_i e^{-\lambda}, & z_i>a_i e^{\lambda}. \end{cases}proxF/ϵKL​(z)i​=⎩⎨⎧​zi​eλ,ai​,zi​e−λ,​zi​<ai​e−λ,ai​e−λ≤zi​≤ai​eλ,zi​>ai​eλ.​
(75)

  • Fixed total mass. If F=ι{⟨r,1⟩=m}\mathsf F=\iota_{\{\langle r,\ones\rangle=m\}}F=ι{⟨r,1⟩=m}​, then prox⁡F/ϵKL(z)=mz/⟨z,1⟩\operatorname{prox}_{\mathsf F/\epsilon}^{\KLD}(z)=m z/\langle z,\ones\rangleproxF/ϵKL​(z)=mz/⟨z,1⟩.

These examples explain why generalized Sinkhorn algorithms remain practical: the expensive operation is still multiplication by K\KK or K⊤\K^\topK⊤, while the model-specific part is a low-dimensional KL-proximal update on a marginal.

Heat Kernels and Hopf--Cole Transforms¶

The Gaussian kernel used by Sinkhorn is also the Euclidean heat kernel. This viewpoint clarifies when entropic OT admits fast grid and surface implementations, and it places soft minima and Hopf--Cole transforms in the same heat-kernel calculus.

Geodesics in Heat¶

On Rd\mathbb R^dRd, the heat kernel for ∂tu=Δu\partial_t u=\Delta u∂t​u=Δu is

ht(x,y)=(4πt)−d/2exp⁡ ⁣(−∥x−y∥24t).h_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\norm{x-y}^2}{4t}\right).ht​(x,y)=(4πt)−d/2exp(−4t∥x−y∥2​).
(76)

Up to normalization, the quadratic Sinkhorn Gibbs kernel is therefore a Gaussian heat kernel with heat time t=ϵ/4t=\epsilon/4t=ϵ/4. A neighboring but distinct construction uses the resolvent of the positive Laplacian. On the line, the kernel of (I−τΔ)−1(I-\tau\Delta)^{-1}(I−τΔ)−1 is exactly proportional to exp⁡(−∣x−y∣/τ)\exp(-|x-y|/\sqrt{\tau})exp(−∣x−y∣/τ​); in higher dimension it is a Yukawa--Bessel kernel with the same exponential tail. Thus one resolvent step gives a Laplace/Yukawa smoothing, while the heat semigroup gives the Gaussian kernel exp⁡(−∥x−y∥2/(4t))\exp(-\norm{x-y}^2/(4t))exp(−∥x−y∥2/(4t)). On a Riemannian manifold or surface MMM, Varadhan’s formula gives

−4tlog⁡ht(x,y)⟶dM(x,y)2(t↓0).-4t\log h_t(x,y)\longrightarrow d_M(x,y)^2 \qquad (t\downarrow0).−4tloght​(x,y)⟶dM​(x,y)2(t↓0).
(77)

This underlies geodesics-in-heat methods Varadhan, 1967Crane et al., 2013. Writing L=−ΔML=-\Delta_ML=−ΔM​ for the positive Laplace--Beltrami operator, one has

e−tL=lim⁡q→∞(I+tqL)−q.e^{-tL}=\lim_{q\to\infty}\left(I+\frac{t}{q}L\right)^{-q}.e−tL=q→∞lim​(I+qt​L)−q.
(78)

Thus a single inverse shifted Laplacian (I+τL)−1(I+\tau L)^{-1}(I+τL)−1 gives a Laplace/Yukawa smoothing, while repeated resolvent steps approximate the Gaussian heat kernel. On a triangulated surface or image grid, LLL is replaced by a discrete Laplacian LhL_hLh​, and one applies sparse linear solves rather than dense Gaussian matrices. This is attractive computationally, but the small-scale limit is delicate: the smoothing length, of order t\sqrt tt​ for heat and τ\sqrt\tauτ​ for one resolvent step, must be resolved by the mesh. If this length is sent to zero faster than the grid spacing, metrication artifacts and inconsistent discretizations can dominate the intended geodesic limit.

show_book_figure("sinkhorn-geodesics-in-heat")

Geodesics-in-heat approximation of the distance to a dense non-convex source curve. One backward-Euler resolvent step with Neumann boundary conditions is followed by a normalized-gradient Poisson solve. Larger resolvent scales stabilize the linear solve but progressively round the non-convex level-set geometry.

Soft Hopf--Lax and Hopf--Cole¶

The Hopf--Lax formula is the Hamilton--Jacobi incarnation of the hard ccc-transform. We use the normalized quadratic cost

c(x,y)=12∥x−y∥2,c(x,y)=\frac12\norm{x-y}^2,c(x,y)=21​∥x−y∥2,
(79)

so that the Hopf--Lax operator applied to an initial datum hhh is precisely

(−h)cˉ(x)=inf⁡y{h(y)+12∥x−y∥2}.(-h)^{\bar c}(x)=\inf_y\left\{h(y)+\frac12\norm{x-y}^2\right\}.(−h)cˉ(x)=yinf​{h(y)+21​∥x−y∥2}.
(80)

The sign only reflects the convention of Definition: ccc-Transform. This is the usual Hopf--Lax formula for the Hamiltonian ∥p∥2/2\norm{p}^2/2∥p∥2/2 Evans, 2010Villani, 2009; other quadratic scalings amount to multiplying the cost by a constant. In the present entropic setting, the parameter of interest is instead the temperature ϵ\epsilonϵ.

The soft version replaces the infimum by a log-sum-exp soft minimum. In the notation of Definition: Continuous Soft ccc-Transforms, and using Lebesgue measure on Rd\RR^dRd,

(−h)cˉ,ϵ(x)=−ϵlog⁡∫exp⁡ ⁣(−h(y)+∥x−y∥2/2ϵ) dy.(-h)^{\bar c,\epsilon}(x) = -\epsilon\log \int \exp\!\left(-\frac{h(y)+\norm{x-y}^2/2}{\epsilon}\right)\,dy .(−h)cˉ,ϵ(x)=−ϵlog∫exp(−ϵh(y)+∥x−y∥2/2​)dy.
(81)

This is a soft ccc-transform of the function −h-h−h, and Laplace’s principle gives (−h)cˉ,ϵ→(−h)cˉ(-h)^{\bar c,\epsilon}\to(-h)^{\bar c}(−h)cˉ,ϵ→(−h)cˉ as ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0 under the usual compactness assumptions on near-minimizers. The same formula is also a heat-kernel formula. If

Gϵ(z)=(2πϵ)−d/2exp⁡ ⁣(−∥z∥22ϵ),G_\epsilon(z)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\norm{z}^2}{2\epsilon}\right),Gϵ​(z)=(2πϵ)−d/2exp(−2ϵ∥z∥2​),
(82)

then

(−h)cˉ,ϵ(x)=−ϵlog⁡(Gϵ∗e−h/ϵ)(x)−ϵd2log⁡(2πϵ).(-h)^{\bar c,\epsilon}(x) = -\epsilon\log\big(G_\epsilon\ast e^{-h/\epsilon}\big)(x) -\frac{\epsilon d}{2}\log(2\pi\epsilon).(−h)cˉ,ϵ(x)=−ϵlog(Gϵ​∗e−h/ϵ)(x)−2ϵd​log(2πϵ).
(83)

Thus a soft quadratic ccc-transform is a Gaussian convolution followed by a logarithm, up to an explicit additive constant independent of xxx. This is the bridge between soft-minimum operators, heat kernels and entropic transport potentials.

Proposition: Soft Quadratic ccc-Transform and Legendre Approximation

Let f:Rd→R∪{+∞}f:\RR^d\to\RR\cup\{+\infty\}f:Rd→R∪{+∞} be such that the integrals below are finite, and introduce the quadratic shift Sf(y)=f(y)−∥y∥2/2\mathsf S f(y)=f(y)-\norm{y}^2/2Sf(y)=f(y)−∥y∥2/2. For ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, define the soft conjugate by applying the soft cˉ\bar ccˉ-transform to the shifted function:

f∗,ϵ(p)=12∥p∥2−(−Sf)cˉ,ϵ(p).f^{*,\epsilon}(p) =\frac12\norm{p}^2-\big(-\mathsf S f\big)^{\bar c,\epsilon}(p).f∗,ϵ(p)=21​∥p∥2−(−Sf)cˉ,ϵ(p).
(84)

Then

f∗,ϵ(p)=ϵlog⁡∫Rdexp⁡ ⁣(⟨p,y⟩−f(y)ϵ) dy,f^{*,\epsilon}(p) =\epsilon\log\int_{\RR^d} \exp\!\left(\frac{\dotp{p}{y}-f(y)}{\epsilon}\right)\,dy,f∗,ϵ(p)=ϵlog∫Rd​exp(ϵ⟨p,y⟩−f(y)​)dy,
(85)

and equivalently

f∗,ϵ(p)=12∥p∥2+ϵlog⁡(Gϵ∗e−Sf/ϵ)(p)+ϵd2log⁡(2πϵ).f^{*,\epsilon}(p) =\frac12\norm{p}^2 +\epsilon\log\big(G_\epsilon\ast e^{-\mathsf S f/\epsilon}\big)(p) +\frac{\epsilon d}{2}\log(2\pi\epsilon).f∗,ϵ(p)=21​∥p∥2+ϵlog(Gϵ​∗e−Sf/ϵ)(p)+2ϵd​log(2πϵ).
(86)

If, for instance, fff is proper, lower semicontinuous and superlinear, then f∗,ϵ(p)→f∗(p)f^{*,\epsilon}(p)\to f^*(p)f∗,ϵ(p)→f∗(p) for every ppp as ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0.

The proof is just completion of squares. Since

inf⁡y{Sf(y)+12∥p−y∥2}=12∥p∥2−f∗(p),\inf_y\left\{\mathsf S f(y)+\frac12\norm{p-y}^2\right\} =\frac12\norm{p}^2-f^*(p),yinf​{Sf(y)+21​∥p−y∥2}=21​∥p∥2−f∗(p),
(87)

this shift turns the Legendre--Fenchel transform into a quadratic cˉ\bar ccˉ-transform. Replacing the hard transform by its soft version gives the definition of f∗,ϵf^{*,\epsilon}f∗,ϵ. Expanding the square yields the log-sum-exp formula, the Gaussian-convolution expression follows from the normalized kernel GϵG_\epsilonGϵ​, and the convergence follows from Laplace’s principle.

Remark: Fast soft Legendre--Fenchel transforms

Proposition Proposition: Soft Quadratic ccc-Transform and Legendre Approximation gives a computational recipe for a smoothed Legendre--Fenchel transform. On a periodic, or sufficiently padded, grid, the term Gϵ∗e−Sf/ϵG_\epsilon\ast e^{-\mathsf S f/\epsilon}Gϵ​∗e−Sf/ϵ in (86) is a Gaussian convolution. It can therefore be evaluated in O(Nlog⁡N)O(N\log N)O(NlogN) operations for NNN grid samples using an FFT. This is not an exact hard discrete Legendre transform, but a regularized approximation whose zero-temperature limit recovers the hard transform by Laplace’s principle. Exact discrete conjugation and lower-envelope algorithms exploit convex-analytic and computational-geometry structure instead; see Lucet’s survey of computational convex analysis and the distance-transform algorithm of Felzenszwalb and Huttenlocher Lucet, 2010Felzenszwalb & Huttenlocher, 2012.

The convolutional route is nevertheless delicate when ϵ\epsilonϵ is small. In fixed precision, the factors e−f/ϵe^{-f/\epsilon}e−f/ϵ or e−Sf/ϵe^{-\mathsf S f/\epsilon}e−Sf/ϵ can underflow or overflow, and the logarithm can amplify small relative convolution errors. Practical implementations therefore use shifts, log-domain evaluations, or stabilized FFT convolutions. In dimension ddd, one can also use the same separability of the Gaussian kernel as in grid Sinkhorn: direct one-dimensional passes give the tensor-product cost (10), namely O(d N1+1/d)O(d\,N^{1+1/d})O(dN1+1/d), while FFT convolutions provide an additional acceleration when boundary conditions and conditioning permit it.

Other Convex Regularizers¶

KL regularization is the case that leads to multiplicative Sinkhorn scalings. Replacing KL by another density-ratio penalty keeps the same transport constraints but changes the scalar law linking the optimal density to the dual potentials.

Let ϕ\phiϕ be an entropy function and define

Lc,ϕϵ(α,β):=min⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫c(x,y)  dπ(x,y)+ϵDϕ(π∣α⊗β).\mathcal L_{c,\phi}^{\epsilon}(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \min_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int c(x,y)\,\d\pi(x,y) + \epsilon D_\phi(\pi|\alpha\otimes\beta).Lc,ϕϵ​(α,β):=π∈Π(α,β)min​∫c(x,y)dπ(x,y)+ϵDϕ​(π∣α⊗β).
(89)
Proposition: Dual and Density Law for ϕ\phiϕ-Regularized OT

Under standard Fenchel--Rockafellar qualification assumptions,

Lc,ϕϵ(α,β)=sup⁡f,g∫f  dα+∫g  dβ−ϵ∫ϕ∗,≥0(f(x)+g(y)−c(x,y)ϵ) dα(x) dβ(y).\mathcal L_{c,\phi}^{\epsilon}(\alpha,\beta) = \sup_{f,g} \int f\,\d\alpha+\int g\,\d\beta - \epsilon \int \phi^{*,\ge0} \left( \frac{f(x)+g(y)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon} \right) \d\alpha(x)\d\beta(y).Lc,ϕϵ​(α,β)=f,gsup​∫fdα+∫gdβ−ϵ∫ϕ∗,≥0(ϵf(x)+g(y)−c(x,y)​)dα(x)dβ(y).
(90)

If the optimal plan has density r⋆= dπ⋆/ d(α⊗β)r^\star=\d\pi^\star/\d(\alpha\otimes\beta)r⋆=dπ⋆/d(α⊗β) and the solution is smooth and interior, then

r⋆(x,y)=(ϕ′)−1(f⋆(x)+g⋆(y)−c(x,y)ϵ).r^\star(x,y) = (\phi')^{-1} \left( \frac{f^\star(x)+g^\star(y)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon} \right).r⋆(x,y)=(ϕ′)−1(ϵf⋆(x)+g⋆(y)−c(x,y)​).
(91)

For KL, ϕ(r)=rlog⁡r−r+1\phi(r)=r\log r-r+1ϕ(r)=rlogr−r+1 and ϕ∗,≥0(s)=es−1\phi^{*,\ge0}(s)=e^s-1ϕ∗,≥0(s)=es−1, recovering the Sinkhorn dual. Other choices replace the exponential law by another scalar transfer function:

ϕ(r)=rlog⁡r−r+1⇒r⋆=es,ϕ(r)=r−log⁡r−1⇒r⋆=(1−s)−1(s<1),ϕ(r)=12(r−1)2⇒r⋆=(1+s)+,s=f⋆⊕g⋆−cϵ.\begin{array}{lll} \phi(r)=r\log r-r+1 &\Rightarrow& r^\star=e^s,\\ \phi(r)=r-\log r-1 &\Rightarrow& r^\star=(1-s)^{-1}\quad(s<1),\\ \phi(r)=\frac12(r-1)^2 &\Rightarrow& r^\star=(1+s)_+, \end{array} \qquad s=\frac{f^\star\oplus g^\star-c}{\epsilon}.ϕ(r)=rlogr−r+1ϕ(r)=r−logr−1ϕ(r)=21​(r−1)2​⇒⇒⇒​r⋆=es,r⋆=(1−s)−1(s<1),r⋆=(1+s)+​,​s=ϵf⋆⊕g⋆−c​.
(92)

Generalized Soft ccc-Transforms¶

The same dual formula yields block-coordinate ascent updates. For fixed ggg, maximizing the dual with respect to the scalar value f(x)f(x)f(x) gives the generalized soft transform

gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ(x)∈argmin⁡u∈R{ϵ∫ϕ∗,≥0(u+g(y)−c(x,y)ϵ) dβ(y)−u}.g^{\bar c,\epsilon,\phi}(x) \in \operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\mathbb R} \left\{ \epsilon \int \phi^{*,\ge0} \left( \frac{u+g(y)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon} \right) \d\beta(y) -u \right\}.gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ(x)∈u∈Rargmin​{ϵ∫ϕ∗,≥0(ϵu+g(y)−c(x,y)​)dβ(y)−u}.
(93)

Equivalently, when ϕ∗,≥0\phi^{*,\ge0}ϕ∗,≥0 is differentiable, u=gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ(x)u=g^{\bar c,\epsilon,\phi}(x)u=gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ(x) is characterized by

∫(ϕ∗,≥0)′(u+g(y)−c(x,y)ϵ) dβ(y)=1.\int (\phi^{*,\ge0})' \left( \frac{u+g(y)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon} \right) \d\beta(y) =1.∫(ϕ∗,≥0)′(ϵu+g(y)−c(x,y)​)dβ(y)=1.
(94)

This equation says that the conditional density induced by the current dual score has unit β\betaβ-mass, hence it is exactly the row-normalization step in dual variables. The update fc,ϵ,ϕf^{c,\epsilon,\phi}fc,ϵ,ϕ is defined symmetrically by exchanging (x,α,f)(x,\alpha,f)(x,α,f) and (y,β,g)(y,\beta,g)(y,β,g). For KL, this reduces to the log-integral soft transform; for Burg or quadratic penalties, the update is still one-dimensional and monotone but no longer a log-sum-exp.

Bregman vs. ϕ\phiϕ-Divergence Regularization¶

The previous construction regularizes OT by a density-ratio divergence. This differs from using a Bregman divergence generated by a convex functional on the space of measures.

Definition: Measure Bregman Divergence

If Φ\PhiΦ is a differentiable convex functional on a convex class of nonnegative measures and ξ\xiξ is a reference measure, the Bregman divergence generated by Φ\PhiΦ is

BΦ(π∣ξ):=Φ(π)−Φ(ξ)−∫δΦ(ξ)  d(π−ξ),B_\Phi(\pi|\xi) \eqdef \Phi(\pi)-\Phi(\xi) - \int\delta\Phi(\xi)\,\d(\pi-\xi),BΦ​(π∣ξ):=Φ(π)−Φ(ξ)−∫δΦ(ξ)d(π−ξ),
(95)

where δΦ(ξ)\delta\Phi(\xi)δΦ(ξ) is the first variation.

Proposition: Dual Comparison

For a fixed product reference ξ=α⊗β\xi=\alpha\otimes\betaξ=α⊗β, Bregman regularization has a dual involving the global conjugate Φ∗\Phi^*Φ∗ and the translated dual coordinate δΦ(ξ)+(f⊕g−c)/ϵ\delta\Phi(\xi)+(f\oplus g-c)/\epsilonδΦ(ξ)+(f⊕g−c)/ϵ. In contrast, ϕ\phiϕ-regularization has the scalar-integral dual above and the pointwise density law

f⋆⊕g⋆−cϵ∈∂ϕ( dπ⋆ d(α⊗β)).\frac{f^\star\oplus g^\star-c}{\epsilon} \in \partial\phi \left( \frac{\d\pi^\star}{\d(\alpha\otimes\beta)} \right).ϵf⋆⊕g⋆−c​∈∂ϕ(d(α⊗β)dπ⋆​).
(96)
Main Idea of the Proof

Write the Bregman-regularized objective, up to constants independent of π\piπ, as

ϵΦ(π)+∫(c−ϵδΦ(ξ))  dπ.\epsilon\Phi(\pi) + \int(c-\epsilon\delta\Phi(\xi))\,\d\pi .ϵΦ(π)+∫(c−ϵδΦ(ξ))dπ.
(97)

Dualizing the marginal constraints and minimizing over π\piπ produces the global conjugate Φ∗\Phi^*Φ∗. Equality in Fenchel’s inequality gives the Bregman optimality condition. The density-ratio dual follows instead from the scalar Legendre formula for Dϕ(⋅∣α⊗β)D_\phi(\cdot|\alpha\otimes\beta)Dϕ​(⋅∣α⊗β).

Proposition: KL is the Common Bregman and ϕ\phiϕ Case

Under natural smoothness assumptions, if a Bregman divergence BΦ(α∣β)B_\Phi(\alpha|\beta)BΦ​(α∣β) equals a ϕ\phiϕ-divergence Dϕ(α∣β)D_\phi(\alpha|\beta)Dϕ​(α∣β) for all positive probability densities, then

ϕ(t)=c tlog⁡t+a(t−1)\phi(t)=c\,t\log t+a(t-1)ϕ(t)=ctlogt+a(t−1)
(98)

for some c≥0c\ge0c≥0 and a∈Ra\in\RRa∈R. Hence the common divergence is a multiple of KL, up to an irrelevant affine term.

Thus the two generalizations lead to different duals and different algorithms. Only for KL do density-ratio regularization and Bregman projection geometry coincide and reduce to multiplicative Sinkhorn scalings.

Sinkhorn Divergences¶

Sinkhorn divergences remove the entropic self-bias while retaining smoothness. They interpolate between OT-like geometry and kernel-like norms, which explains their statistical behavior.

Entropic Bias¶

The raw Sinkhorn cost is biased: for ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, minimizing Lcϵ(α,β)\mathcal L_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)Lcϵ​(α,β) over β\betaβ does not generally return β=α\beta=\alphaβ=α. In the large-temperature limit, the raw value behaves like a product interaction:

Proposition: Large-Temperature Entropic Bias

Assume ccc is bounded and continuous. Then

Lcϵ(α,β)→∬c(x,y)  dα(x) dβ(y)as ϵ→+∞.\mathcal L_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) \to \iint c(x,y)\,\d\alpha(x)\d\beta(y) \qquad \text{as }\epsilon\to+\infty.Lcϵ​(α,β)→∬c(x,y)dα(x)dβ(y)as ϵ→+∞.
(99)

For c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2, minimizing this large-temperature limit over β\betaβ collapses toward a Dirac at the mean of α\alphaα.

Sinkhorn Divergences¶

The standard debiasing subtracts the two self-interaction energies. This cancellation removes the large-temperature attraction toward the independent coupling; positivity is a separate property, proved below through the positive-definite kernel associated with e−c/ϵe^{-c/\epsilon}e−c/ϵ.

Definition: Sinkhorn Divergence

For ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, the debiased Sinkhorn divergence is

L‾cϵ(α,β):=Lcϵ(α,β)−12Lcϵ(α,α)−12Lcϵ(β,β).\overline{\mathcal L}_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \mathcal L_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) - \frac12\mathcal L_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\alpha) - \frac12\mathcal L_c^\epsilon(\beta,\beta).Lcϵ​(α,β):=Lcϵ​(α,β)−21​Lcϵ​(α,α)−21​Lcϵ​(β,β).

Lemma: Entropic Dual Cost at Optimum

Let (fα,β,gα,β)(f_{\alpha,\beta},g_{\alpha,\beta})(fα,β​,gα,β​) be optimal dual potentials. Then

Lcϵ(α,β)=∫fα,β  dα+∫gα,β  dβ.\mathcal L_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) = \int f_{\alpha,\beta}\,\d\alpha + \int g_{\alpha,\beta}\,\d\beta.Lcϵ​(α,β)=∫fα,β​dα+∫gα,β​dβ.
(101)
Proof

At optimality,

1=∫e(fα,β(x)+gα,β(y)−c(x,y))/ϵ dβ(y)1 = \int e^{(f_{\alpha,\beta}(x)+g_{\alpha,\beta}(y)-c(x,y))/\epsilon} \d\beta(y)1=∫e(fα,β​(x)+gα,β​(y)−c(x,y))/ϵdβ(y)
(102)

for α\alphaα-almost every xxx. Therefore the exponential penalty term in the dual integrates to zero, and the dual value reduces to the two linear potential terms.

Proposition: Asymptotics of Sinkhorn Divergences

Assume the two measures are supported on the same space and that ccc is bounded, continuous, nonnegative, and satisfies c(x,x)=0c(x,x)=0c(x,x)=0. Then

L‾cϵ(α,β)→Lc(α,β)(ϵ→0),\overline{\mathcal L}_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) \to \mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta) \qquad (\epsilon\to0),Lcϵ​(α,β)→Lc​(α,β)(ϵ→0),
(103)

and

L‾cϵ(α,β)→−12∫c  d(α−β)⊗ d(α−β)(ϵ→+∞).\overline{\mathcal L}_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) \to - \frac12 \int c\,\d(\alpha-\beta)\otimes\d(\alpha-\beta) \qquad (\epsilon\to+\infty).Lcϵ​(α,β)→−21​∫cd(α−β)⊗d(α−β)(ϵ→+∞).
(104)
Remark: Large-temperature Hilbertian limit

If −c-c−c defines a conditionally positive definite kernel, the large-temperature limit in Proposition Proposition: Asymptotics of Sinkhorn Divergences is the square of a Hilbertian kernel norm. A typical example is c(x,y)=∥x−y∥pc(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^pc(x,y)=∥x−y∥p for 0<p<20 < p < 20<p<2, which corresponds to the energy-distance kernel. This kernel norm is the dual of a homogeneous Sobolev norm.

Complex Epsilon¶

The Sinkhorn temperature is usually a positive real number: positivity makes the Gibbs kernel positive, gives the entropy a convex meaning, and underlies the Hilbert-metric and monotone convergence arguments of the next chapter. Once the equations are written as exponential fixed-point equations, however, ϵ\epsilonϵ can also be regarded locally as a complex variable. This does not produce a positive coupling or a contraction theorem; it produces a holomorphic branch of the same scaling equations near any positive real temperature.

Measure fixed point¶

Let α∈P(X)\alpha\in\mathcal P(X)α∈P(X) and β∈P(Y)\beta\in\mathcal P(Y)β∈P(Y). Whenever the following integral operators are well defined, set, for ϵ∈C∖{0}\epsilon\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}ϵ∈C∖{0},

Kϵ(x,y)=exp⁡(−c(x,y)/ϵ).K_\epsilon(x,y)=\exp(-c(x,y)/\epsilon).Kϵ​(x,y)=exp(−c(x,y)/ϵ).
(108)

The measure-theoretic scaling equations are the infinite-dimensional counterpart of matrix scaling. They are best written for the density of the complex coupling with respect to α⊗β\alpha\otimes\betaα⊗β:

dπϵ(x,y)=u(x)Kϵ(x,y)v(y) dα(x)dβ(y).d\pi_\epsilon(x,y) = u(x)K_\epsilon(x,y)v(y)\,d\alpha(x)d\beta(y).dπϵ​(x,y)=u(x)Kϵ​(x,y)v(y)dα(x)dβ(y).
(109)

Prescribing the two marginals gives the fixed-point equations

u(x)∫YKϵ(x,y)v(y) dβ(y)=1for α-a.e. x,v(y)∫XKϵ(x,y)u(x) dα(x)=1for β-a.e. y.u(x)\int_Y K_\epsilon(x,y)v(y)\,d\beta(y)=1 \quad \text{for }\alpha\text{-a.e. }x, \qquad v(y)\int_X K_\epsilon(x,y)u(x)\,d\alpha(x)=1 \quad \text{for }\beta\text{-a.e. }y.u(x)∫Y​Kϵ​(x,y)v(y)dβ(y)=1for α-a.e. x,v(y)∫X​Kϵ​(x,y)u(x)dα(x)=1for β-a.e. y.
(110)

Formally, Sinkhorn alternation becomes

u(k+1)(x)=(∫YKϵ(x,y)v(k)(y) dβ(y))−1,v(k+1)(y)=(∫XKϵ(x,y)u(k+1)(x) dα(x))−1.u^{(k+1)}(x)= \left(\int_Y K_\epsilon(x,y)v^{(k)}(y)\,d\beta(y)\right)^{-1}, \qquad v^{(k+1)}(y)= \left(\int_X K_\epsilon(x,y)u^{(k+1)}(x)\,d\alpha(x)\right)^{-1}.u(k+1)(x)=(∫Y​Kϵ​(x,y)v(k)(y)dβ(y))−1,v(k+1)(y)=(∫X​Kϵ​(x,y)u(k+1)(x)dα(x))−1.
(111)

If a branch of the logarithm is fixed along the local continuation and u=ef/ϵu=e^{f/\epsilon}u=ef/ϵ, v=eg/ϵv=e^{g/\epsilon}v=eg/ϵ, this is equivalently

f(x)=−ϵlog⁡ ⁣∫Yexp⁡ ⁣(g(y)−c(x,y)ϵ)dβ(y),g(y)=−ϵlog⁡ ⁣∫Xexp⁡ ⁣(f(x)−c(x,y)ϵ)dα(x).f(x)=-\epsilon\log\!\int_Y \exp\!\left(\frac{g(y)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon}\right)d\beta(y), \qquad g(y)=-\epsilon\log\!\int_X \exp\!\left(\frac{f(x)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon}\right)d\alpha(x).f(x)=−ϵlog∫Y​exp(ϵg(y)−c(x,y)​)dβ(y),g(y)=−ϵlog∫X​exp(ϵf(x)−c(x,y)​)dα(x).

For real positive ϵ\epsilonϵ, this is the usual Sinkhorn fixed point. For complex ϵ\epsilonϵ, the same formulas should be read as local analytic identities, not as a positivity statement.

Remark: Local, not global, complex scaling

The theorem is local around a positive real point. It does not rule out complex singularities, branch changes, or zeros of the denominators in (117) farther away. On compact intervals ϵ∈[ϵmin⁡,ϵmax⁡]⊂(0,+∞)\epsilon\in[\epsilon_{\min},\epsilon_{\max}]\subset(0,+\infty)ϵ∈[ϵmin​,ϵmax​]⊂(0,+∞), the local neighborhoods can be patched into a tube around the interval, but one should not expect a global single-valued continuation on C∖{0}\CC\setminus\{0\}C∖{0} without additional assumptions.

The local continuation can be visualized on a finite histogram problem. The real part changes only at second order in the imaginary perturbation, so the left panel displays the centered quantity ℜ(fϵ0+iη−fϵ0)\Re(\fD_{\epsilon_0+i\eta}-\fD_{\epsilon_0})ℜ(fϵ0​+iη​−fϵ0​​). Since the potentials enter only through exponentials, the complex logarithm has to be followed on a continuous local branch; this is a display convention, while the coupling itself is defined by the exponential formula.

−kϵ22sDϵx2−kϵ22tDϵy2+kϵDϵxy.-\frac{k_\epsilon^2}{2sD_\epsilon}x^2 -\frac{k_\epsilon^2}{2tD_\epsilon}y^2 +\frac{k_\epsilon}{D_\epsilon}xy .−2sDϵ​kϵ2​​x2−2tDϵ​kϵ2​​y2+Dϵ​kϵ​​xy.
(132)

Comparing this with pϵx2+qϵy2−(x−y)2/ϵp_\epsilon x^2+q_\epsilon y^2-(x-y)^2/\epsilonpϵ​x2+qϵ​y2−(x−y)2/ϵ gives kϵ/Dϵ=2/ϵk_\epsilon/D_\epsilon=2/\epsilonkϵ​/Dϵ​=2/ϵ, hence Dϵ=kϵϵ/2D_\epsilon=k_\epsilon\epsilon/2Dϵ​=kϵ​ϵ/2, and then precisely the displayed formulas for pϵp_\epsilonpϵ​ and qϵq_\epsilonqϵ​. This comparison also explains why the scaling exponents need not be negative: the decaying factor e−(x−y)2/ϵe^{-(x-y)^2/\epsilon}e−(x−y)2/ϵ is part of the full coupling density. Nonzero Gaussian means add affine terms to the scaling exponents; the quadratic recurrence and the cross-covariance formula are unchanged.
